description: On April 4 1881, A.B. Goodman was bound from Baltimore, MD, to New Berne, NC, with a cargo of guano. Snow and intense winds washed one of its crew overboard. Eventually the vessel ran aground on Diamond Shoals with four men clinging to its rigging. As the ship began to break apart, rescuers from Creeds Hill Life-Saving Station set out in a surfboat fighting opposing current and a strong wind. It took several hours before they could rescue the crewmembers aboard A.B. Goodman.

On August 16, 1899, during the San Ciriaco hurricane, Aaron Reppard grounded in the surf while carrying a cargo of coal. The eight-man crew climbed into the rigging. Life savers from Chicamacomico, Gull Shoal, and Little Kinnakeet Life-Saving Stations gathered on the beach, attempting to fire their Lyle Guns to reach the vessel. In the storm, one crewman fell from a mast, his leg caught in a rope, and was battered against the mast. As the ship broke apart, another crewman died. Captain Osker Wessel jumped into the sea in an attempt to reach the beach but was forced to turn around in the heavy surf and drowned. The foremast collapsed, and the remaining men fell into the breakers. Three men survived.

description: Ario was a tanker built in 1920. During WWII, Ario operated on a course through the Gulf of Mexico and up the East Coast.

On March 15, 1942, Ario was traveling 11 miles southwest of Cape Lookout, North Carolina. The ship was unarmed and alone when U-158 attacked. Ario managed to send a radio distress signal confirming the attack, leading to the survival of 30 out of 38 members aboard.

Today, the remains of the site believed to be Ario are located inshore in relatively shallow waters, approximately 60 feet deep. The site is broken apart, due to the post-war efforts to clear navigable areas and its proximity to the nearby shore, making it a source of confusion regarding its identity.

description: On December 24, 1899, steamship Ariosto was bound for Germany carrying cottonseed, lumber, cotton, and wheat. The ship began experiencing rough winds and seas and grounded in the breakers. Captain R.R. Barnes sent out a distress call and received an answer from the nearest Life-Saving Station.

Ignoring Life-Saving Service instructions to stay aboard the vessel, the captain sent out a lifeboat and pinnance. The two vessels capsized in the rough seas. Two men swam back to the ship and several were dragged from the surf by lifesavers. Those still on board the ship, including the captain, were rescued, but 21 crewmen were buried on Ocracoke Island.

The ship was abandoned for a later salvage attempt, and all the crew were rescued and taken to Morehead City, N.C.

description: Atlas was a tanker built in 1916.

On April 9, 1942, the unescorted and unarmed Atlas was sailing from Texas to New Jersey loaded with over 84,000 barrels of gasoline. Early that morning, as Atlas passed Cape Lookout, U-552 fired a torpedo that struck the ship’s side. The explosion did not ignite the cargo. The crew of eight officers and 26 men abandoned the ship in three lifeboats. U-552 moved in closer and fired a second torpedo, striking Atlas, creating a fireball that caused the ship to burn from stem to stern. Two of the three lifeboats got away without harm. The other lifeboat with 11 crew members drifted into the burning gasoline on the water. They were ordered to jump overboard before the fire swept over them, but two men drowned as they tried to escape the flames.
Today, the wreck site supports a diverse ecosystem.

While sailing along Diamond Shoals, Australia came in contact with U-332, which shot a single torpedo. The torpedo struck the side of Australia, causing a large explosion in multiple areas, killing four men instantly. The rest of the crew abandoned the ship and were rescued.
Australia eventually sank completely. At the wreck location today, most of the remains of Australia are covered up by shifting sands, with site conditions varying from year to year.

Both ships are significant to American military history, as they represent the physical remains of the only World War II naval battlefield off the East Coast of the United States where both the aggressor and its victim are present.

description: British Splendour carried fuel during World War II, and in early April 1942, the tanker left Texas to meet with a British convoy in Nova Scotia.

On the night of April 7, 1942, British Splendour cruised off the coast of North Carolina, followed by U-552. A single torpedo was fired by U-522, striking the port side near the engine room, causing British Splendour to be immediately disabled. 12 crew members were killed instantly, and fire spread throughout the ship. The fuel in the cargo hold ignited and engulfed the ship. The rest of the surviving crew members were ordered to abandon ship, and within two hours, the vessel sank.

When British Splendour sank, the vessel settled upside down. The wreck rests in about 100 feet of water. At that depth, with shifting sands and variable currents, site conditions vary over the course of a year, creating an ever-changing environment.

description: On the night of April 5, 1942, tanker Byron D. Benson and two other ships slowly moved north with a cargo of crude oil, while unknowingly being stalked by U-552. U-552 attacked, shooting a torpedo that struck Byron D. Benson on the starboard side. This caused the crude oil cargo to gush from the opening and quickly spread a fire.

The crew was ordered to abandon ship, but with the loss of the starboard side lifeboats, the remaining boats were overfilled. Amid panic to abandon the burning ship, the engines were never shut down, allowing Byron D. Benson to continue to make way while the crew attempted to escape. In spite of many difficulties, 27 of the 37 crewmembers survived the attack. Byron D. Benson did not sink for three days.

Today, Byron D. Benson rests in approximately 105 feet of water, located in an area that typically has lower visibility than other sites. Some features are discernable such as the completely burned out midsection.

description: On March 2, 1942, Caribsea departed from Cuba bound for Virginia with 3,600 tons of manganese ore.

Shortly after 2:00 am, on March 11, 1942, Caribsea was suddenly struck by a torpedo from U-158. The vessel began to sink in just two minutes, leaving no time to secure lifeboats. Crew members had to jump into the ocean, forcing survivors to cling to the remaining wreckage, and after drifting for approximately ten hours, those surviving were spotted and picked up by the steamship Norlandia. Only 7 out of 28 crew members survived. Family members of crew members of Caribsea found floating wreckage on the shore of Ocracoke Island just days later, thus confirming for the community Caribsea’s tragic fate.
Today, the wreck rests in 90 feet of water. Caribsea is a popular diving destination and sustains a rich marine ecosystem.

description: The Swedish freighter Carl Gerhard was bound for Florida in the fall of 1929 carrying a load of plasterboard. Off the New England coast, the ship began to veer off course as bad weather made it difficult to navigate. The ship had been lost for five days when it ran aground and hit the sunken hull of Kyzikes, another freighter that wrecked in the same spot just two years prior.
A local spotted the vessel and summoned Coast Guard crews. The seas were too rough to launch a boat, so a Lyle Gun was fired from the shore to rescue the crew in a breeches buoy.

Today, Carl Gerhard rests offshore as part of the "Triangle Wrecks." The site consists of the remains of Carl Gerhard and two sections of Kyzikes. These sites are popular with fishermen, snorkelers, and diver.

description: On January 29, 1921, the Cape Lookout Lighthouse keeper reported seeing Carroll A. Deering offshore. A crew member yelled that the ship had lost its anchors and it continued sailing on. Two days later, the Coast Guard found the ship grounded on Diamond Shoals, abandoned.

When the Coast Guard was able to reach the ship, the crew and their navigational equipment, belongings, documents, and lifeboats were all gone.  Strangely, dinner was still on the stove and the captain’s cabin was a mess.  The cause of the wreck and fate of the crew remain a mystery.
A few months later, the ship was dynamited so it wouldn’t be a navigational hazard.

description: Central America, known as the Ship of Gold, was a sidewheel steamer that operated between Central America and the East Coast of the U.S. during the 1850s. The ship sank in a hurricane in 1857 on the way back from California, along with 425 of 578 passengers and crew and 30,000 pounds of gold. The tragedy of 425 deaths was overshadowed by the loss of gold, which made it the greatest economic disaster in US maritime history and contributed to a global panic.

The shipwreck was located in 1988, and coins and artifacts were salvaged.  Shortly after, 39 insurance companies filed suits, claiming the damages they paid in the 19th century for the lost gold entitled them to the salvage.  However, treasure hunters claimed that the wreck had been abandoned, and were awarded 90% of the salvage.

description: In January 1942, City of Atlanta departed from New York heading to Savannah carrying almost 3,000 tons of cargo and passengers. To avoid a possible U-boat attack, the crew hugged the coastline and ran with navigational lights dimmed. U-123 spotted and tracked City of Atlanta as it approached the North Carolina coast.

In the early hours of January 19, 1942, U-123 fired one torpedo which hit City of Atlanta and set off a massive explosion, scattering debris and capsizing City of Atlanta. Only 3 of 46 crew members survived, the largest loss of life off North Carolina during the Battle of the Atlantic. After six hours clinging to wreckage, the three survivors were rescued by Seatrain Texas.

description: CSS Curlew was an iron-hull steamboat built in 1856 for Edenton plantation owner Dr. Thomas Warren for passenger and freight service. Warren sold the vessel to the Confederate States Navy when the Civil War began. Curlew actively patrolled Pamlico Sound and Hatteras Inlet between 1861 and 1862, helping in the capture of the Union supply boat Fanny at Chicamacomico on October 1, 1861.

On February 8, 1862, Curlew was part of the “Mosquito Fleet” that attempted to repel Union forces at Roanoke Island. During the battle, Curlew was hit by two shells and had to be run aground so she would not sink. After salvaging her gun, Curlew was set on fire the next day and exploded as Confederate forces retreated.

description: During WWI on August 6, 1918, the cargo ship Merak was sailing past Diamond Shoals on its way to Brazil when it came under attack by German submarine U-140.

The crew of LV-71, hearing shelling, reported by radio that an unknown vessel was under fire near their location. U-140 intercepted the report and broke off its attack to stop the source of the radio transmissions. Coming within range of LV-71, U-140 began firing with its deck gun. The 12-man crew of LV-71 lowered their lifeboat and rowed away as U-140 sank their doomed ship. After seven hours of rowing, the crew of LV-71 reached Cape Hatteras.

description: E.S. Newman was on its way from Rhode Island to Virginia in October 1896 when it ran aground in a storm off Pea Island.

Beach patrols had been halted due to the storm, but a lookout at Pea Island Life-Saving Station spotted a flare from E.S. Newman. Keeper Richard Etheridge, a freedman and veteran of the Civil War, and his all-Black life-saving crew, the first in the nation, set out to rescue the ship’s passengers.

However, heavy seas made it impossible to launch a surfboat or mount a Lyle Gun.  The life-saving crew decided to send out their two best swimmers with a line and take turns bringing back the survivors one-by-one.
The Pea Island life-savers did not receive awards for their valor until 1996, when they were posthumously awarded the highest honor of gold lifesaving medals.

description: In August 1750, Spanish treasure ship El Salvador was traveling with six other Spanish ships, including Nuestra Señora De Soledad and Nuestra Señora de Guadalupe, from Columbia to Spain. A storm forced the ships into the Gulf Stream where El Salvador, Soledad, and Guadalupe were driven ashore along the Outer Banks. El Salvador was badly broken up and buried in several feet of sand with only the rigging still visible above the water. Only four members of the crew survived the wreck.

Archival documents indicate that El Salvador was carrying four chests of gold coins and sixteen chests of silver coin. Most of the treasure aboard the other Spanish ships was salvaged but El Salvador’s cargo was never recovered.

description: The tanker Empire Gem was travelling from Texas in January 1942 with a cargo of 10,000 tons of spirits/kerosene.

A few miles southeast of the Diamond Shoals Lightbuoy, Empire Gem was sailing with another tanker, Venore. U-66 saw both vessels and fired two torpedoes. Both torpedoes hit Empire Gem's aft starboard tank causing a large explosion and fire. Despite SOS calls for help and the attempt to launch lifeboats, the intense heat kept crewmembers from being successful. Of the 51 crewmembers, only two survived.

Empire Gem continued to motor for three more hours at full speed before the engines finally stopped. The tanker broke in half. Today, Empire Gem rests at 160 feet and rests almost completely upside down.

The U-boat fired one torpedo which hit the vessel, causing it to slowly sink. The crew of 55 made it safely to the lifeboats and were picked up by an American Q-ship which had witnessed the attack.

In 1944, a Navy salvage team set explosives inside the sunken vessel to reduce the remains to help aid navigation. Additionally, the site was wire dragged to break up any submerged remains. Today, there are few visible remains of Empire Thrush.

description: Ephraim Williams was bound home from Georgia with a cargo of pine lumber in December 1884 when it encountered heavy weather. It became waterlogged and drifted helplessly. The crews of Durant, Creeds Hill, and Cape Hatteras Life-Saving Stations saw the ship but could not send aid because of the terrible storm.

At daylight the storm continued, but surfboats from several stations launched to attempt a rescue. However, the rough seas and sandbars kept the life-savers from reaching the vessel.  The Cape Hatteras Life-Saving crew was finally able to cross the sandbar with perfect timing at the peak of a wave. They then rowed five miles and rescued the crew.
Seven Gold Lifesaving Medals were awarded to the lifesavers from Cape Hatteras and Creed's Hill stations.

description: Esso Nashville was an oil tanker which was traveling alone and unarmed from Texas to Connecticut when in the early morning hours of March 21 it was struck by two torpedoes from U-124. The first torpedo caused very little damage, but the second torpedo struck amidships.
The entire crew of 38 abandoned ship into the four lifeboats that were on board. All 38 survived.

For several hours after the attack, the tanker held together, but finally broke completely in two. The bow section sank but the stern section continued to float and was eventually salvaged for further fitting and armament modification. The ship ultimately returned to active service on March 16, 1943, less than a year after the attack.

description: Beginning as a luxury yacht owned by William L. Harness, ex-USS Cythera was donated in the beginning of World War I for the war effort. After the war, the vessel returned to the Harkness family.

Years later, after the attack on Pearl Harbor during WWII, the Harkness family sold the ship back to the US Navy for one dollar. Cythera was converted into a patrol craft and re-commissioned as USS Cythera. Cythera departed for Pearl Harbor but on May 2, 1942, it was spotted by U-402. U-402 fired three torpedoes, breaking Cythera in half. Cythera sank rapidly with only two survivors of the crew of 71. U-402 picked up the two survivors, who were taken to Germany and placed in a prisoner-of-war camp.

description: At the outbreak of hostilities in WWI, the German cruiser SMS Geier (Vulture) found itself in hostile Pacific waters and sailed to the neutral US port of Honolulu. However, the US Navy detained the ship for three years. When the US entered the war, the ship was seized.

After a refit, the ex-USS Schurz spent most of its active life conducting escort duty and coastal patrols. In the early morning of June 21, 1918, SS Florida was under steam without running lights and crashed into Schurz. It penetrated 12 feet into the hull, killing one crewmember and injuring 12. Schurz sank rapidly.
A Navy investigation laid blame on the faulty navigation of Florida and placed the responsibility on its captain. The name Schurz was struck from the Navy list.

description: During WWII, fishing trawler Cohassett was pressed into service and refitted several times by the US Navy as USS YP-389. In June 1942, it was sent to patrol the Hatteras minefield and warn any merchant vessels that may stray off course.

On June 16, German U-boat U-701 arrived in the area and attacked ex-USS YP-389 with its deck gun, resulting in an exchange of surface gunfire between the two vessels, which lasted for over an hour and a half. Six of the crew died during the battle. As ex-USS YP-389 sank, the remaining crew abandoned ship in lifejackets since their lifeboats had been destroyed in the gun battle. They floated in the water until the next morning when they were rescued by two Coast Guard cutters.
In 1973, the remains of ex-USS YP-389 were identified during a survey to search for the Civil War ironclad USS Monitor.

description: During WWII on June 11, 1942 F.W. Abrams, carrying over 90,000 barrels of crude oil unarmed and alone, sought refuge in a minefield that had been created to offer Allied vessels safety from German U-boats patrolling off Cape Hatteras.

On its way out of the minefield, F.W. Abrams lost sight of its escort in a heavy rain and made a change of course to head out to sea. Explosions from two mines rocked the ship. The captain believed they were under attack from a U-boat, and had the crew abandon ship. The captain remained on board for a few days, hoping the vessel could be salvaged. However F.W. Abrams slowly sank and finally submerged on June 15th.
Today, the wreck rests at approximately 85 feet deep. Due to the site's location in shallow water, it was a navigational hazard and several destructive techniques were applied to the site.

Shipwrecks.notes: scuttled by uboat crew.  Captain Holbrook, of the HATTIE DUNN, said his vessel was sunk on May 25 and he and his crew were taken prisoner. [The Pensacola Journal, Tuesday, 4 June 1918]
description: During WWI on May 23, 1918, the schooner Hattie Dunn was bound for South Carolina when it was fired upon and boarded by U-151. The crew was given 10-minutes to gather their personal effects while bombs were placed on the schooner. As they were taken aboard the U-boat, an explosion sank Hattie Dunn. It was the first US vessel sunk by a foreign power since the War of 1812.

Hattie Dunn crew was soon joined by captured seamen from Hauppage and Edna. One of the 23 prisoners recounted that “the politeness of the Germans soon got on everyone’s nerves. Captain von Nostitz und Jänckendorff wanted everything done correct right down to the scratch of a pen.” The Germans even gave each captain a receipt for his ship.
The prisoners spent 10-days aboard the U-boat while it sank another six vessels.  They were released into captured  lifeboats and rowed for 22 hours until they were spotted by a passing steamer.
In 2014, a wreck was identified as a possible candidate for Hattie Dunn.

The captain and owner of the vessel had to be convinced to abandon the ship as there was no hope of freeing it from the shoals. description: Bedfordshire was a small British deep sea fishing vessel designed for arctic trawling. At the onset of WWII, many trawlers were requisitioned by the Royal Navy, refitted, and used for military operations. After the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, 24 vessels including Bedfordshire were transferred for service in US waters where the U-boat war had refocused.

In the early hours of May 12, 1942, U-558 spotted HMT Bedfordshire on patrol off Cape Lookout. U-558 fired two torpedoes that both missed and went unnoticed by Bedfordshire's crew. U-558 repositioned and fired a third torpedo that hit its mark. A massive explosion sank Bedfordshire immediately. There were no survivors among the 37 crewmembers on board. The first indication that anything was amiss came when six crewmembers washed up on beaches along the coast.
Today, the vessel remains a sovereign immune state vessel belonging to the United Kingdom and is a military wartime grave.

description: Senateur Duhamel was a British fishing vessel that was converted for anti-submarine patrol in WWII. The ship was transferred to the United States Navy in 1942 and was sent along with 23 other British converted trawlers to help patrol the East Coast.

While on patrol near Beaufort Inlet, the crew of HMS Senateur Duhamel spotted another ship, USS Semmes, about a mile away. As there was a slight fog, they couldn’t identify the ship and flashed a message, "what ship?" The light temporarily blinded USS Semmes's crew and before they could reply, the bow of the ship crashed into Senateur Duhamel. Senateur Duhamel began to sink and was eventually lost, but the crew was rescued.
The ship sank in about 65 feet of water with part of its mast sticking out, making it a navigational hazard. To remove the hazard, the US Navy blasted and wire dragged the site.

description: On October 8, 1837, Home was traveling the route to Charleston when it encountered the hurricane “Racer’s Storm.” Overnight, a leak sprung, due to damage sustained when she had earlier run aground at port.

The next evening, the ship was steered towards shore in order to beach the ship, but she was so waterlogged that she ran aground 300 feet out.  The pounding surf broke up the vessel as the 130 people on board abandoned ship into the deadly waters.

The ship held only two life preservers.  Only 40 people made it to shore.  The beach was covered with fragments of the boat—and bodies—for miles.  Congress soon passed legislation requiring an equal number of life preservers for each person on board a US flag vessel.

description: During WWII on July 15, 1942, merchant convoy KS-520 consisting of 19 merchant ships and five military escorts was attacked. In the hours that followed, a series of miscommunications resulted in the damaged merchant ships mistakenly navigating into the Cape Hatteras minefield while attempting to reach port. Two merchant vessels, Chilore and J.A. Mowinckel, accidentally detonated mines and had to be abandoned within the minefield.

Over the next couple of days, several channels were swept so that tugs could reach the damaged merchant vessels and tow them to port. On July 19, Keshena was one of two tugs dispatched to tow the merchant vessels out of the minefield. Keshena moved out of the safe channel and struck a mine. The tug sank within ten minutes. Two members of Keshena's crew were killed in the accident and fifteen were rescued.
At a depth of 85 feet, much of Keshena is intact and can easily be circled several times during a single dive.

description: In early December 1927, Kyzikes left Baltimore towards Spain with a cargo of crude oil when it was caught in a storm. The captain turned south towards North Carolina to avoid the heavy winds. However, the ship took on water and the boiler tubes burst, disabling the vessel. Kyzikes lost power and drifted until it ran aground on a shoal. The vessel broke in two and four crewmen perished. The rest of the crew were trapped on board. Over 23 men from Kill Devil Hills and surrounding lifesaving stations mounted a large operation and rescued the crew.

description: At the outbreak of World War II, Lancing and other Norwegian ships were ordered to the nearest Allied or neutral port. Lancing was directed to America and supported the war effort.

In March 1942, Lancing was en route to New York with 8,802 tons of fuel onboard. On the morning of April 7, 1942, Lancing was suddenly torpedoed without warning by U-552. The torpedo blew up a portion of the deck and created a large hole in the side. The engine room flooded, killing one crewman. The radio equipment was damaged so no distress signal was sent.
The rest of the crew made it into lifeboats and rafts and were picked up by other ships in the area.
Today, a single large hole is still visible in Lancing's hull.

Shipwrecks.notes: friendly fire incident, then sunk by uboat
description: During WWII on the night of March 18, 1942 cargo ship Liberator saw a large tanker burning near Cape Lookout. Radio traffic indicated that the U-boat responsible for the attack might still be in the area. Liberator's naval gun crew immediately went to full alert and the vessel accelerated to full speed out of the area.

Miles away, USS Dickerson's radar crew picked up a fast-moving surface contact near the burning tanker. Thinking that the radar contact was a U-boat, USS Dickerson approached Liberator running blacked-out at nearly full speed. Liberator's crew opened fire at the unknown approaching vessel, killing several sailors and injuring the captain. As he lay wounded on the bridge, he ordered USS Dickerson to make full speed away. He died the next day of his injuries.

Meanwhile, the commotion had attracted the attention of U-332. The next morning, as Liberator was speeding away from the area thinking that they had battled a U-boat, U-332 fired two torpedoes. The two hits killed five crew members in the explosion and set the cargo on fire. The ship sank in less than 30 minutes. 31 crewmembers were later rescued.

description: During WWII in early April 1942, Malchace was traveling alone carrying a load of soda ash from Louisiana, to New Jersey. On the morning of April 9, U-160 hit Malchace with a torpedo. The captain ordered the crew to abandon ship. All but one of the 29 crewmembers made it safely to the lifeboats. As they were rowing towards shore, they witnessed the explosion and sinking of the tanker Atlas by U-552. Later that morning, they were spotted and rescued by Mexican tanker Faja de Oro.

Two crew members were killed in the explosion and the compartments quickly filled with water.
The crew of Manuela abandoned ship. 23 crewmen made it into a lifeboat and 17 others jumped overboard and climbed onto three life rafts.

Manuela remained afloat following the attack. A salvage crew from the US Coast Guard boarded the ship to prepare it to be towed. There, they discovered one seriously wounded crewman on deck. As Manuela was under tow to Morehead City, it sank. Today, the wreck rests at 160 feet deep near Ocracoke.

Shipwrecks.notes: Very interesting story of faked paperwork, etc
description: On February 10, 1983, Marine Electric was sailing from Virginia to Massachusetts with a cargo of 24,800 tons of granulated coal. The ship was soon fighting a severe storm and raced to reach port amidst 25-foot waves and winds gusting more than 55 miles per hour. In the early morning of February 12, the crew noted that the ship’s bow was riding low in the water. Multiple mayday calls were made to the Coast Guard. Marine Electric soon capsized, killing 31 of 34 crewmen. The three survivors drifted for 90 minutes in the frigid waters of the Atlantic before being rescued.

Investigations discovered that Marine Electric had left port with gaping holes in its deck plating and hatch covers. The Chief Mate testified that he had noted the problems but the shipping company had not fixed them. Investigators discovered that much of the paperwork supporting Marine Electric′s seaworthiness was faked.

The wreck resulted in important maritime reforms: tightening inspection standards, requiring mandatory survival suits for winter North Atlantic runs, and creating the now famous Coast Guard rescue swimmer program.

Most of the crew was asleep in their bunks. As the crew scrambled to the lifeboats, U-432 began to shell the ship to ensure that it sank.
All 39 crew members made it safely away from the sinking freighter in three lifeboats, and were rescued by passing tanker John D. Gill and Coast Guardsmen from Big Kinnakeet Station.

description: On January 31, 1878, the steamship Metropolis ran aground off Currituck Beach in rough seas from a recent storm. The wreck gained national attention due to its large loss of life: 85 deaths out of 245 passengers. The wreck of Metropolis and the wreck of USS Huron, just a few months earlier, led to the US government providing proper funding for the US Life-Saving Service. By June of that year, the US Life-Saving Service was fully funded and began construction of new life-saving stations, proper training of personnel, and hiring of staff to keep the stations open year-around.

description: During WWI on August 16, 1918 near Wimble Shoals Light Buoy, German submarine U-117 was laying mines when its crew spotted the British tanker Mirlo. A single torpedo from U-117 hit the tanker.

Coast Guardsmen from Chicamacomico Station spotted the explosion and launched their surfboat into the rough waters.  They encountered Captain William’s lifeboat about 5-miles from shore.  Motoring further into the burning waters, the Coast Guardsmen rescued survivors clinging to a second lifeboat, as well as survivors packed aboard a third.  42 of 51 crew had been rescued.

Upon reaching shore, Captain Williams wrote that he and his men were injured “with burnings and very little clothing on.”  He recalled that “the eyes of all the life saving crew were all bloodshot, which was caused by their getting so close to the fire as to be partly gassed and smoke into their eyes.”

description: During WWII in March of 1942, Naeco was transporting 97,000 barrels of fuel oil alone and unarmed from Texas to New Jersey. On March 23 near Cape Hatteras, U-124 attacked Naeco. The first torpedo either missed or was a dud. A second torpedo ignited the cargo of fuel oil and engulfed the deck house and bridge. Burning fuel spread across the water. All hands in the bridge area and forward were killed. The Chief Engineer shut down the engines and turned on the steam smothering system to try to stop the burning fuel.

The explosion had destroyed all the forward lifeboats, but at least ten crewmembers made it safely into another lifeboat. Several nearby US vessels rushed to the scene and rescued the survivors from the lifeboat, two more from the water, one survivor on the burning stern, and one survivor clinging to a partially destroyed life raft. 24 crew members lost their lives in the attack.
Naeco continued to burn and eventually broke in two. Today, the two halves can be found about a mile apart on the seabed.

description: On December 27, 1904, Northeastern was traveling from Texas to Philadelphia with a crew of 22 when it was blown off course in a gale. Just before midnight, it grounded on Diamond Shoals. The water was still dangerously rough, prompting the keeper of Hatteras Station, Patrick H. description: During WWII, in late January 1942, Norvana left Cuba bound for Philadelphia carrying a cargo of sugar and 29 crew members. It was lost near Cape Hatteras and no distress signal was sent.

description: During WWI on August 14, 1918, the crew of the tanker O. B. Jennings sighted an incoming torpedo. They took evasive action and dropped smoke to hide their menuevers. German submarine U-140 surfaced and shelled the tanker’s approximate position with its deck gun. O. B. Jennings returned fire, but was soon struck by two shells, killing one and wounding several crewmembers, and disabling the engine.

The crew abandoned ship in several lifeboats. U-140 then sunk O. B. Jennings and captured the crew for interrogation. The crew refused to identify the captain, who had changed into other clothes. Suspiciously, the tanker’s second officer, who claimed to be Belgian, spoke to the submarine’s commander in German and was taken aboard. Eventually the crew of O. B. Jennings were set free and were later picked up by a US Navy vessel.

The tanker’s Belgian second officer had, in fact, been imprisoned in the engine room with other prisoners of war. Over the course of several weeks he witnessed the sinking of LV-71, Merak, and other vessels, as well as tense engagements with allied Navy vessels. He was brought to Germany and held as a prisoner of war until the end of WWI several months later.

description: On October 16, 1964, the freighter Omar Babun ran into a gale on the way to Havana carrying ready-to-assemble equipment for a cement factory and a steel forging plant.
In the storm the cargo shook loose, tearing away the deck supports and ripping its hull.  The captain beached the ship 300 yards from shore and the crew was rescued by the Coast Guard.

Professional salvage companies pronounced the ship a total loss.  But a Havelock, NC Buick dealer, fascinated with shipwrecks, chartered a plane to inspect the wreck.  Then he flew to New York City and bought the hull for $3,500 and made a deal with the insurance companies for 30% of the salvage.  With a team of five employees and 25 locals, he bulldozed a sand roadway to the wreck and recovered the cargo, including a 23-ton steel press.

description: During WWII on March 18, 1942, Papoose was traveling alone toward Texas when it was spotted by U-124 near Cape Lookout. The U-boat fired a single torpedo into the tanker's port side. The explosion penetrated the fuel tanks and ruptured the engine room bulkheads, killing two crew members.

As the crew abandoned ship in two lifeboats, a second torpedo hit the drifting tanker, tearing a large hole at the water line. The tanker rolled to the side but remained adrift for two days. The survivors were picked up by USS Stringham.

Though there has been confusion regarding the identification of the wreck, NOAA believes it has identified Papoose through historical research and with the assistance of the recreational diving community. Shipwrecks.notes: Theodosia Burr
description: During the War of 1812, in early January 1813, the schooner Patriot was on its way to New York City. Theodosia Burr Alston, the daughter of former Vice President Aaron Burr and the wife of the governor of South Carolina, was on board. On January 2, the schooner was stopped by the British Fleet near Cape Hatteras but allowed to pass.

However, Patriot never arrived in New York City and was presumed lost at sea. Aaron Burr came to believe that his daughter had perished. In 1833, an Alabama newspaper reported that a man on his deathbed confessed that he had participated in the capture of Patriot and the murder of all those on board. However, in 1869, a doctor attending to an old Banker noticed a woman’s portrait on her wall. She told him that the Bankers had discovered an abandoned ship near Nags Head with a woman’s belongings and the portrait on board. Today, scholars believe that Patriot was likely lost in a gale, reported by the British fleet on January 2.

description: During the Civil War on November 5, 1861, neutral French corvette Prony was caught in a gale while returning from observation of the Union Navy‘s blockade of the port of Charleston.

During the storm, Prony ran aground on a shoal. The pilot believed the ship could be refloated at high tide and left for help. The captain of Prony sent a boat ashore but a strong surf prevented it from returning. The crew lightened their stores, trying to refloat the vessel. Four US ships approached but told the crew it would only be possible to assist at high tide. The ships left and never returned. The Confederate privateer Winslow was also on its way to assist Prony but struck a sunken vessel.
Eventually, the 140 crew members of Prony were rescued and placed on board the Confederate steamers Seabird and Ellis. Prony was burned to prevent it from falling into the hands of the US Navy.

description: During WWI on August 19, 1918 the elegant passenger liner Proteus was on its way from New Orleans with 95 passengers and crew. Proteus was running without its navigational lights due to U-boats patrols in the area. Nearby, Standard Oil tanker Cushing, painted in a camouflage pattern, was also running without navigational lights.

Around midnight, the two ships collided. Cushing tore a hole in Proteus and the order was given to abandon ship. The only casualty was a crewmember who jumped overboard and drowned. The survivors were picked up by Cushing. In a few hours Proteus sank to the bottom.
Today, the wreck site is under 125 feet of water and sustains an incredible number and diverse array of fish.

description: In mid-June 1838, the steamer Pulaski left Charleston, South Carolina with about 150 people aboard, from some of the wealthiest families in the Southeast.

On the night of June 14th, its boilers exploded. Sprays of steam killed some passengers immediately.  The lifeboats were in poor condition, and one sank immediately. description: La Concorde was a French slave ship used to transport 1,265 African men, women, and children from West Africa to the New World to be sold into slavery. In 1717, the pirate Edward Teach, also known as “Blackbeard,” captured La Concorde and refitted it as his flagship Queen Anne's Revenge

Less than a year later in May 1718, Blackbeard blockaded the port of Charleston, South Carolina, demanding food, money, and supplies. Shortly after, his fleet entered Beaufort Inlet where Queen Anne's Revenge ran aground. The ship's stores were moved off and the fleet was disbanded. Some historians have suggested that Blackbeard deliberately grounded the ship as an excuse to disperse his crew.
The wreck of Queen Anne's Revenge was discovered in 1996 and today many artifacts are undergoing conservation and are on display at the North Carolina Maritime Museum.

description: Before the war, the tanker San Delfino worked routes from Mexico, the Gulf of Mexico, and the East Coast of the United States to the United Kingdom. At the outbreak of World War II, San Delfino underwent conversions to add multiple deck guns and machine guns, in order to defend itself from any U-boat.

On April 9, 1942, as U-203 patrolled the waters, it spotted San Delfino traveling alone from Houston, Texas to Halifax, Nova Scotia and on to the United Kingdom. U-203 fired one torpedo, striking the starboard side near the number two or number three tank, instantly igniting some of the 11,000 tons of aviation fuel carried by San Delfino. A second explosion erupted, possibly from either the ammunition cargo or the weapons on board. Flames ignited all over the vessel. The call to abandon ship was made and two lifeboats were lowered. One of the lifeboats got caught in the current and was dragged into a pool of burning fuel, killing the 24 crew members and four gunners in the boat. The master, 19 crew members, and two gunners in the other life boat were picked up by HMS Norwich City (FY-229) and taken to Morehead City, North Carolina. 28 out of 50 crew members lost their lives because of the attack.

description: On February 9, 1905 the schooner Rawson was transporting lumber from South Carolina to New York when it ran aground in rough seas. One crewman was washed overboard and disappeared into the surf. As the ship began to break apart, the crew moved to the highest part of the ship.

A dense fog prevented the surfmen on watch at Cape Lookout Life-Saving Station from spotting the ruined schooner until the next day. The life-saving crew, most of them sick with influenza, launched their surfboat but were unable to reach the wreck.  They decided to attempt a rescue the next day and spent the night in their surfboat at anchor.  The next afternoon, the wind and sea had calmed enough to allow them to reach the wreck and rescue the remaining survivors.

The life-saving crew had spent more than 24 hours in their surfboat during a storm with no food or water, and with most of the surfmen sick with influenza.  Keeper William H. Gaskill and the surfmen of Cape Lookout Station were awarded the Gold Life-Saving medal "for heroic daring" during the rescue.

description: On March 24, 1891, Strathairly was traveling from Cuba to Baltimore with a cargo of iron ore when it encountered dense fog and ran aground.

The crew signaled for help and was answered with a red Coston flare from a surfman on patrol from Chicamacomico Life-Saving Station. The Chicamacomico crew arrived at the wreck site an hour later and tried to shoot a line through the dense fog, but it fell short.
Eventually the rough seas broke the steamer in two and smashed its lifeboats. The life-savers struggled to communicate with the crew and reach the wreck.  7 of 26 men were saved.
Today the wreck is located in 20-30 feet of water off shore.

description: During WWII on May 9, 1942 U-352 attacked USCGC Icarus which was on an antisubmarine patrol off Cape Lookout. Several crewmembers emerged from the conning tower but Icarus began delivering heavy machine-gun fire, killing several of the crew. Icarus left the area to await instructions and returned to the site an hour later and collected 33 survivors, one of whom died shortly after. Before U-576 could attack, a US Coast Guard cutter picked up a radar contact. The Coast Guard crew dropped eight depth charges. Then, U-576 fired four torpedoes, hitting Chilore, J.A. Mowinckel, and Bluefields.

U-576 surfaced and the Armed Guard crew on the merchant ship Unicoi opened fire. Two US Navy Kingfisher aircraft straddled U-576 with more depth charges and sent it to the bottom of the sea with all 45 crew members.

description: During WWII on July 7, 1942, U-701 was patrolling off Cape Hatteras on the surface when an Army Air Force Hudson plane dropped three depth charges, causing significant damage. Two groups of men managed to escape the submarine as it sank to the bottom. These 36 survivors drifted with the Gulf Stream for 49 hours. All but seven drowned. The survivors were rescued by a Coast Guard seaplane and became Prisoners of War (POWs).

The wreck of U-701 was discovered in 1989 by sport diver Uwe Lovas. The wreck sits in approximately 110 feet of water in the shifting sands and currents where the Gulf Stream and Labrador current collide off Cape Hatteras. Lovas contacted U-701’s captain Horst Degen and assured him that the location would be kept a secret so that his comrades would not be disturbed. The site was rediscovered in 2004 following a hurricane and made more accessible to the diving community.

description: During WWII on April 13, 1942, U-85 was sitting in shallow water off Bodie Island Lighthouse waiting for targets. Just after midnight, destroyer USS Roper was approaching the area when it detected a weak radar contact at 2700 yards.

As Roper closed in to 300 yards, the crew saw the track of a torpedo narrowly missing them. Roper turned its searchlights on U-85 and put it under heavy fire from machine guns and 3-inch deck guns. The German crew was cut down before they could man their own deck guns. A well-aimed 3-inch shell breached the pressure hull just aft of the conning tower. As the U-boat sank, survivors jumped into the water.

Believing that U-boats operated in packs, as they did in other regions, Roper left the survivors in the water and dropped an additional 11 depth charges to ensure that U-85 was sunk. The depth charges killed the entire surviving crew of U-85.

description: During WWII on September 14, 1944, USCGC Bedloe and its sister ship Jackson were ordered to aid the merchant vessel George Ade, which had been disabled by a torpedo attack. Conditions were rapidly deteriorating due to an approaching hurricane.

As the storm worsened, George Ade sent out an SOS, but neither Bedloe nor Jackson were able to respond. The ships were battered by winds over 100 miles per hour and waves over 100 feet high. After several hours battling the waves both Bedloe and Jackson capsized

All of the crew escaped into life rafts as the ship was sinking, but were forced to endure the storm and exposure for over two days. The crews of both Jackson and Bedloe, each unaware of the terrible fate that had befallen the other ship, awaited rescue from the other. Finally, Bedloe’s 12 surviving crewmen were rescued by a US Navy minesweeper.

Resting in 140 feet of water, the wreck of USCGC Bedloe lays on its side, almost fully intact. The forward deck gun remains in place and the shell boxes on the forward section near the gun still have intact shells inside. Today the wreck teems with marine life including sand tiger sharks, amberjacks, black sea bass, and tautogs.

description: On November 23, 1877 USS Huron was on its way Havana, Cuba to survey the surrounding coast. A storm, combined with a small error in the ship's compass, caused Huron to run aground. Because of the strong surf and cold temperatures, most of the crew remained on the ship. However, Life-Saving Stations were closed until December. Many of the men lost their strength in the storm and were washed overboard.

The wreck of USS Huron and the wreck of the Metropolis, just a few months later, led to the US government providing proper funding for the US Life-Saving Service. By June of 1888, the US Lifesaving Service was fully funded and began construction of new Life-Saving Stations, proper training of personnel, and hiring of staff to keep the stations open year-around.

After the wreck, the ship's cannons and much of its machinery were salvaged. Today, the wreck site is located 250 yards from the beach. Divers who visit the site can see a wide variety of sea life as they swim over the remains of the historic warship.

description: During WWII on January 23, 1942, Venore was transporting 8,000 tons of ore alone when it was overtaken by the tanker Empire Gem.

That night, as the two ships approached Diamond Shoals, U-66 spotted them. As U-66 lined up to fire at Venore, Empire Gem suddenly changed course, running right in front of U-66's torpedoes and was struck. Venore quickly navigated away from the burning vessel at full speed. U-66 hit Venore with a torpedo, setting the stern on fire. Some of the crewmen lowered two lifeboats, which hit the water and instantly tore apart both the boat and its occupants. A third boat launched successfully, but with only two men on board. A second torpedo hit, causing the ship to list sharply and the main deck to completely submerge.
The remaining crew abandoned the ship in the last lifeboat as the ship finally capsized and sank. Only 24 of 41 crewmembers survived.
Although a shipwreck site is charted in the recorded vicinity of the sinking, Venore has never been definitively located.

description: On May 8, 1903, Vera Cruz VII was traveling from the Cape Verde Islands to Massachusetts carrying 399 passengers and 214 barrels of whale oil. While trying to enter Ocracoke Inlet it ran aground on Dry Shoal Point and sent out a distress call. When the crew from Portsmouth Life-Saving Station arrived, the captain requested that they transfer all 23 women, 3 children, and 10 men to the station while the rest remained on board.

The following morning, the seas were becoming dangerous and the life-savers requested the aid of local villagers. Together they used the station’s two surfboats to rescue the remaining 371 passengers and crew. The rescue remains the largest single vessel rescue in North Carolina history.

Rumors of smuggling operations surround Vera Cruz VII. Ocracoke Inlet is far outside the shipping route from Cape Verde Islands to Massachusetts. Additionally, only 225 of the 399 passengers were listed on the ship's manifest. Some sources suggest that the ship was wrecked on purpose in an attempt to smuggle immigrants and liquor into the United States.

In the early morning hours of March 19, U-124 fired two torpedoes, one of which hit its mark. W.E. Hutton immediately sent a distress signal and the crew lowered the lifeboats. U-124 fired another torpedo which struck under the bridge, buckling the decks and overturning the pilothouse. In just a few minutes, W.E. Hutton was a fiery inferno. The crew abandoned ship and began to row towards the shore.

A year after W.E. Hutton sank, the merchant vessel Suloide crashed into its wreckage and sank to the bottom. The US Navy dispatched US Coast Guard Cutter Vigilant to clear the wreckage to make the area safe for navigation.

U-701 fired two torpedoes, one which hit Rockefeller, spraying oil and fire across the ship. The crew panicked and abandoned ship without orders. description: ECU and CSI (Coastal Studies Institute) partnered together to investigate a shipwreck that was located near Rodanthe, NC, known to locals as the “Pappy Lane Wreck”.

Drawings and blueprints of the wreck created by ECU students and staff revealed that it shared design similarities with Landing Craft Support amphibious assault vessels from WWII. The team at ECU poured over historical records of amphibious craft looking for vessels that were bought as surplus after the war. A tentative identification is that the remains belong to LCS-123.

Records show that the Landing Craft saw extensive combat in the Pacific during World War II.   After the war, the vessel was purchased by the Hunt Oil Company, based out of Hampton Roads, VA, and converted into a fuel barge.  In the late 1960s it may have run aground.

description: In response to an ever-increasing number of shipwrecks and the activities of “salvagers”, Diligence III & Governor Williams conducted a survey in 1806 from Cape Hatteras to Cape Fear.

On September 30, a hurricane descended on the region. Despite jettisoning the guns and cutting away masts to avoid capsizing, Diligence III was driven nearly a mile away where it collided with a small schooner already aground on a shoal. Diligence’s crew scrambled aboard the grounded schooner before Diligence III sank, drowning one crewmember. To the south, Governor Williams sank at anchor. Three crewmembers were trapped below deck and drowned.
Despite the loss of four crew and two ships, the survey was completed. This initial success led Congress to authorize surveys of the entire US coast.

description: During WWII on June 2, 1943, USS PC-565 was escorting a convoy when it obtained a contact with a submerged U-boat. Assuming that the U-boat was preparing to attack the convoy and would be at periscope depth, PC-565 dropped depth charges set for a depth of 100 feet.
Onboard U-521, Kapitänleutnant Klaus Bargsten was reading in his bunk when the sound operator rushed in to report propeller noises directly overhead. Suddenly the depth charges went off.
Instruments were shattered, the lights went off, the motors stopped, rudder and diving planes were rendered useless, and water entered the control room.  Bargsten ordered the U-boat to surface.
As U-521 surfaced, PC-565 went to full speed intending to ram, while its 20mm gun opened fire and scored several hits on the U-boat’s conning tower.

Before 521 could fully surface, it began to quickly sink. PC-565 dropped a final depth charge. A single survivor was pulled from the sea, Kapitänleutnant Klaus Bargsten, who had emerged from the conning tower hatch and given the order to abandon ship, too late.

description: On February 28, 2004, Bow Mariner was transporting 3.2 million gallons of ethanol, 200,000 gallons of fuel oil, and 53,000 gallons of diesel oil.

Crew members were ordered to open the tanks for cleaning, a major safety violation.  Released vapors were likely ignited by a spark.  Massive explosions ripped apart the hull and instantly killed nearby crewmembers.

The third officer asked the Captain about transmitting a Mayday signal, but was ignored.  The third officer left to send the Mayday signal himself.  When he returned, he found that the captain and other officers had jumped overboard and were swimming away from the ship.  No general alarm had been sounded, nor an announcement made.

Bow Mariner spilled its entire cargo of ethanol and oil as it sank. The loss of Bow Mariner is considered one of the worst chemical tanker disasters in history. Only 6 of 27 crewmembers were found alive by the Coast Guard.

description: On May 12, 1911, Merida was en route to New York from Vera Cruz, Mexico. Passengers included many Americans and Mexicans fleeing the violence of the Mexican Revolution. Its cargo reportedly included over a thousand bars of silver and copper.

Just after midnight, Merida encountered a fog bank and collided with the fruit boat Admiral Farragut. The engines and electrical dynamo were disabled. Before the batteries were discharged, Merida’s wireless operator was able to send a distress signal.

Sleeping passengers were awakened in a panic, but the captain and crew calmed the crowds and managed to disembark everyone on the ship’s lifeboats and rafts. As Merida sank, the passengers and crew were picked up by the relatively unscathed Admiral Farragut.
Over the next one hundred-plus years, bad weather and other challenges have thwarted any attempts to salvage the silver and copper bars believed to be buried in the wreck.

description: During the Civil War in June 1862, the Confederate blockade runner Modern Greece was attempting to evade Federal ships and enter the Cape Fear River. As it sped along the shoreline, USS Cambridge and USS Stars and Stripes opened fire. Just a half-mile from the protection of Fort Fisher’s guns, Modern Greece ran aground. Rather than have its cargo fall into Union hands, the guns of Fort Fisher sank the stranded vessel.

Modern Greece was thought to be completely destroyed until 1962 when a storm uncovered the wreck. Over the next two years, the North Carolina Department of Archives and History and the US Navy joined forces to salvage over 100,000 individual artifacts.

description: During the Civil War on September 30, 1864, blockade runner Condor attempted to run the Union blockade around Wilmington, NC, carrying cargo and Confederate spy Rose O’Neal Greenhow. Under pursuit by USS Niphon, Condor was forced to swerve to avoid the blockade runner Night Hawk which had been driven aground only two nights beforel. Condor ran at full speed onto the inlet bar and stuck fast. The pursuing USS Niphon was driven off by protective fire from Fort Fisher’s guns. Rose Greenhow, fearing for her life if captured by the Union, demanded to be put ashore immediately. The small boat capsized in the attempt and she drowned in the surf.
On December 3, 1864, after weeks of working to salvage Condor’s cargo, the wreck’s remains were used as target practice for Fort Fisher’s 150-pound Armstrong gun crews.
Since the 1970s the site has been investigated by archeologists and was designated the state’s second Heritage Dive Site.

description: During WWII on January 30, 1942, a lookout on the tanker W. L. Steed spotted what he thought was a small fishing craft on the port bow. The captain determined that it was a German U-boat and radioed for help. The U-boat quickly dove before a Navy patrol plane could take a look.
W. L. Steed’s crew of 38 quickly abandoned ship into four lifeboats. They watched as U-103 fired 17 shells into the stern of the tanker with its deck gun, and departed.

The lifeboats drifted apart and the ill-clad merchant sailors began to succumb to the cold.  Three of the lifeboats were picked up by different vessels over the next 10 days, but only six survivors remained, two of whom died in hospital.  A tanker came across the fourth lifeboat off Cape Hatteras on February 17th.  It was empty.

description: On August 30, 1920, submarine USS S-5 was undergoing trials. As the submarine dove, a crewmember was distracted and didn’t close a valve in time, causing the torpedo room to flood. The submarine settled 180’ deep on the ocean floor.

The crew decided to apply air to the aft ballast and fuel tanks.  The submarine tipped on its nose as the crew held fast and loose objects fell the length of the submarine.  The aft was now sticking above the waves.  After 36 hours, the crew was able to make a small 3-inch hole in the hull.

Steamship Alanthus spotted the tip of the submarine and was able to provide an air pump and fresh water. Another passing steamer, General G. W. Goethals, provided tools to enlarge the hole and rescue S-5’s crew.
The next day, as the battleship USS Ohio was towing S-5, the lines parted and it sank. The US Navy attempted to salvage the wreck twice without success.
The location of the wreck was unknown until a NOAA survey ship discovered it in 2001.

description: The CSS Raleigh was a Conference ironclad built to break the Union blockade around Wilmington, NC during the Civil War.

On the evening of May 6, 1864, CSS Raleigh set off on its first mission to escort a blockade runner out to sea. In the darkness of the blockade, CSS Raleigh and several Union vessels played a game of cat and mouse.

At dawn, CSS Raleigh dueled and attempted to ram approaching Union vessels, but its engine could not give it sufficient speed. In frustration, CSS Raleigh returned to Fort Fisher but ran aground on a sandbar inside New Inlet. At low tide, the ironclad was now unsupported and broke in half. Confederate salvage crews recovered the cannons, boilers, and other materials.
In 1974, a team of archeologists from the NC Division of Archives and History and students identified the buried wreck.

description: In the winter of 1698 HMS Swift was anchored near Point Comfort, Virginia. Captain Nathaniel Bostock departed to seek supplies.
Swift soon became threatened by ice and ran aground, forcing the crew to abandon ship. But as they waited for help on shore, Swift refloated and drifted away.

Captain Bostock and the crew tracked Swift to the Outer Banks, where it had become buried in the sand. Local colonists plundered the ship and fired into its hull with its own gun to prevent it from sailing again.

The plunderers had also destroyed official correspondence on board the vessel.  Historians have speculated that perhaps the Bankers feared that the documents contained allegations or evidence of their complicity with pirates.
